title: Key-Value Store
topic: System Design Deep Dive: Key-Value Store

intro.title: Distributed Key-Value Store
script: Welcome to a system design deep dive on a **distributed key-value store** in the style of Amazon's **Dynamo**.

intro.title: Functional requirements
script: A key-value store is the simplest database there is: you put a value under a key and get it back later. Making it span **hundreds of machines**, stay writable through failures, and answer in milliseconds is where the design lives.
We'll design it the way Dynamo was designed: for something like a **shopping cart**, where losing a write costs money and an error page costs more. Let's agree on what it must do.

cards.title: Get and put by key
script: The API is just **get**, **put** and **delete** by primary key. Values are **opaque blobs** up to about a megabyte; the store doesn't know or care that they're carts. That simplicity is what lets the rest of the design scale.

cards.title: Always writable
script: Writes are **never refused** because some nodes are down or the network is split. A customer who clicks add to cart during an outage should see it work. This is the requirement that shapes everything else.

cards.title: Tunable consistency
lines: N replicas, R reads, W writes
script: Callers choose their trade-off: how many **replicas** to keep, and how many must answer a **read** or a **write**. One table can favor speed and availability, another can favor reading the latest write.

cards.title: Detect and resolve conflicts
lines: Concurrent versions are kept, not lost
merged by the app, or last-write-wins
script: Since we accept writes everywhere, two updates to the same key can happen **concurrently**. The store must **detect** that and keep both versions, then let the application merge them, or fall back to last-write-wins where that's good enough.

cards.title: Elastic membership
lines: only a small share of keys moves
script: We must be able to **add or remove nodes** while serving traffic, with only a proportional slice of the data moving and no manual resharding.

cards.title: Self-healing
script: The cluster **notices** failed nodes by itself, routes around them, and **repairs** replicas that missed writes, without an operator getting involved for every reboot.

outOfScope.title: Out of scope
lines: Range scans and secondary indexes  ·  Multi-key transactions  ·  Linearizable reads  ·  Auth and multi-tenancy  ·  Byzantine faults
script: Out of scope: **range scans and secondary indexes**, since we hash keys and lose their order; **transactions** across keys; **linearizable** reads, which need consensus like Raft or Spanner and are a different design; **auth and multi-tenancy**; and **Byzantine** faults, since we trust our own nodes.

intro.title: Non-functional requirements
script: Now the qualities. For a store like this they are the whole problem: availability and latency first, and consistency as something we can **tune**, not something we assume.

cards.title: Scale
script: Assume **a million operations a second** at peak, about 70% reads, over **10 billion keys** averaging around 10 kilobytes: roughly **100 terabytes** of data before replication.

cards.title: Latency
lines: p99.9 < 10 ms for get and put
script: Gets and puts must finish in **under 10 milliseconds at the 99.9th percentile**. We target the tail, not the average, because one page view may call the store dozens of times, so the slow outliers are what users actually feel.

cards.title: Availability
script: At least **four nines**, and in particular a failed replica, or even a failed rack, must not make writes fail.

cards.title: Durability
lines: An acked write survives node loss
script: Once we say OK, the write must survive losing a machine or even a whole **availability zone**, so it's stored on **three replicas** in three zones.

cards.title: Consistency
lines: R + W > N to read your writes
script: **Eventually consistent** by default: replicas may briefly disagree but converge. Callers that need to read their own writes can ask for overlapping read and write quorums.

cards.title: Decentralized
script: Every node runs the same code with the same responsibilities: **no master**, no special node whose failure stops the cluster. Machines of different sizes should be able to carry proportionate load.

estimates.title: Back-of-the-envelope
script: Some numbers. 10 billion keys at about 10 kilobytes is **100 terabytes**; three replicas make it **300**. At about 4 terabytes of usable disk per node, that's roughly **a hundred nodes**, more with headroom.
A million operations a second, each touching three replicas, is **3 million replica operations** a second, or about **30 thousand per node**, which is comfortable for one machine with SSDs.
And two numbers we'll meet later: with **256 virtual nodes** each, the ring has about **25,000 tokens**; and gossip, at one round a second, reaches all hundred nodes in about **seven rounds**.

takeaway.title: What shapes the design
lines: No master, nodes come and go → consistent hashing with virtual nodes, gossip membership
Writes are never refused → sloppy quorums, hinted handoff, vector clocks
p99.9 < 10 ms → wait for the fastest W or R of N replicas; LSM-tree storage
script: So three decisions follow. With no master and a changing cluster, we place data by **consistent hashing** and spread membership by **gossip**. Since writes must never be refused, we use **sloppy quorums**, **hinted handoff** and **vector clocks**, resolving conflicts later instead of preventing them. And for the tail latency, we wait only for the **fastest replicas** and store data in a write-optimized **LSM tree**.

slides.title: Start: one node
script: Let's start with the simplest key-value store there is: our **cart service** calls **get** and **put** on a single **KV server**, which keeps a hash table on disk. A put writes the value under its key; a get looks the key up. One machine, one copy, and it's perfectly consistent, because there's only one place a value can live.

It fails every one of our requirements, though. One machine can't hold **100 terabytes** or serve **a million operations a second**, and when it dies, the carts are gone. So we need many machines, and the first question is which machine owns which key.

slides.title: Shard by hash mod N
script: The obvious answer is to **hash the key and take it modulo the number of nodes**: node = hash(key) mod N. A good hash spreads keys evenly, every client can compute the owner without asking anyone, and there's no directory to keep up to date.
With three nodes, each one gets a third of the keys and a third of the traffic. It looks great until the cluster has to change size.

slides.title: Adding a fourth node
script: Our data grows, so we add a **fourth node**. Now the formula is hash mod 4 instead of hash mod 3, and for most keys the answer changes.
A key stays put only when its hash mod 3 happens to equal its hash mod 4, which is about **one key in four**. The other three quarters have to move, all at once, while we're serving traffic.

slides.title: How many keys move?
script: Here are six keys. Going from 3 to 4 nodes, only two keep their owner; the rest move. At 300 terabytes that's over **200 terabytes** of data shuffling across the network just to add one machine, and the same thing happens when a node dies and N shrinks.
We need a mapping where adding or removing one node moves only **that node's share**, about 1/N of the keys, and nothing else.

slides.title: Consistent hashing: the ring
script: That mapping is **consistent hashing**. Picture the output of the hash function, say 0 to 2^128, bent into a **ring**. Each node hashes its own id to get a **token**, a position on the ring, and it owns the arc of the ring that ends at its token.
The arrows show the clockwise direction. Six nodes, six arcs, and every node can compute the whole picture from the list of tokens, so there's still no directory to ask.

slides.title: Finding a key's home
script: To find a key, hash it onto the same ring and **walk clockwise** to the first token. Our key **cart:42** lands in the arc between F and A, so **Node A** owns it.

Now add a node, say G between F and A. G takes over only the part of A's arc that lies before G's token; every other key stays exactly where it was. Adding or removing one node moves **about 1/N** of the data, and only between ring neighbors, which is exactly the property we wanted.

slides.title: One token per node isn't enough
script: But one token per node has real problems. Random tokens give **uneven arcs**, so one node can own two or three times its fair share, and a hot arc becomes a hot node.

Failure is worse: when a node dies, its whole arc falls onto **one neighbor**, which doubles that neighbor's load at the worst possible moment. And it can't express that a new machine has twice the disk of an old one.

items.detail: random tokens give some nodes 2–3× their fair share of keys
a dead node's whole arc lands on its clockwise successor
a new node streams all its data from one or two neighbors
a node with 2× the disk still gets one arc

slides.title: Virtual nodes
script: The fix is **virtual nodes**: each physical node takes **many tokens**, say 256, scattered around the ring. With about a hundred nodes that's roughly 25,000 small arcs, and the law of large numbers evens out everyone's share to within a few percent.

When a node fails, its 256 small arcs are picked up by many different neighbors, so the load spreads across the cluster. A bigger machine simply gets more tokens. In our diagram each box is a physical node holding 256 vnodes.

slides.title: Replicate to the next nodes
script: One copy isn't durable, so every key is stored on **N = 3** nodes. Keep walking clockwise past the owner: cart:42 lives on **A, B and C**. That ordered list is the key's **preference list**, and A, the first healthy node in it, acts as the **coordinator** for the request.
The coordinator writes locally and sends the write to the other two replicas, which is what the new arrows show.

slides.title: The preference list
script: A few rules make the preference list useful. With vnodes, the next tokens clockwise may belong to the **same physical machine**, so we skip ahead until we have N **distinct** nodes, and ideally three different racks or availability zones.

The list is also **longer than N**; the extra nodes are stand-ins for when one of the first three is down, as we'll see shortly. And since every node knows the ring, any node can compute any key's list locally.

items.detail: the first N distinct nodes hold the replicas; the first healthy one coordinates
several vnodes in a row may belong to one physical node
3 replicas in 3 availability zones survive losing a whole zone
the extra nodes stand in when a replica is down
every node knows the ring, so there is no lookup service

slides.title: Who coordinates a request?
script: How does the request reach Node A? One option is a plain **load balancer** that sends it to any node, which forwards it to the coordinator. That keeps clients simple but costs an **extra hop** and some latency.

The other is a **partition-aware client library** that downloads the ring and talks straight to the coordinator. That's one hop, which matters at p99.9, so our cart service uses the library; external or simpler clients go through the load balancer.

slides.title: Quorum writes: W = 2
script: The coordinator doesn't wait for all three replicas. We pick a **write quorum W**: the put succeeds as soon as **W = 2** replicas, counting the coordinator itself, have it on disk.

Here A writes locally and B acknowledges, so the client gets its OK; C's acknowledgment arrives later and nobody waits for it. Waiting for the **fastest two of three** is what keeps tail latency down: one slow or garbage-collecting replica doesn't slow the request.

steps.note: W = 2: done after the fastest two

slides.title: Quorum reads: R = 2
script: Reads mirror writes. The coordinator asks the replicas and answers once **R = 2** have replied. If they disagree, it returns the **newest** version, or all the versions if it can't tell which is newer.

Why 2? With **R + W > N**, any two replicas we read overlap any two we wrote in at least one node, so a read always sees the latest acknowledged write, as long as the same three nodes are involved. Hold on to that caveat.

steps.note: R + W > N: every read quorum overlaps every write quorum

slides.title: Tuning N, R and W
script: N, R and W are **knobs**, set per table or even per request. **2, 2 of 3** is the balanced default: reads see the latest write, and we tolerate one slow or failed replica on both paths.

A read-heavy catalog might use **R = 1, W = 3** for the fastest reads; a write-heavy log might use **W = 1**. And **R = 1, W = 1** gives the lowest latency and highest availability at the price of reading stale data. This tunability is the heart of the Dynamo design.

slides.title: Sloppy quorum and hinted handoff
script: Now **Node C becomes unreachable**: it crashed, or a switch dropped it. A strict quorum would still work here with A and B, but if B failed too, strict quorums would start **rejecting carts**, and our first requirement is that writes are always accepted.
So we use a **sloppy quorum**: the write goes to the first N **healthy** nodes in the preference list. **Node D** takes C's copy, stored with a **hint** that says it really belongs to C.

slides.title: Hinted handoff
script: Here's the flow. The coordinator's write to C times out, so it sends the same write to D, the next node in the preference list, marked **"for C"**. D keeps it in a separate **hints** store and counts toward W, so the client still gets its OK.
D also watches the membership state. When C comes back, D **replays** the hint to C and deletes its copy. The write was never refused, and it ends up where it belongs.

slides.title: The replica comes back
script: C is back on the ring, and the dashed arrow is D **handing off** the hinted writes it held. C's own arrows return with it.

Hinted handoff covers **short outages**, minutes to hours. Hints are capped, and if D itself dies before replaying them, they're lost. So it's a fast path back to consistency, not a guarantee; we'll need something stronger for that.

slides.title: The price of always writable
script: Let's be honest about what we've given up. With a sloppy quorum, the nodes we write to may not be the nodes we later read from, so **R + W > N no longer guarantees** that a read sees the latest write.

Worse, during a network partition **two clients can update the same cart** on different sides, and both writes succeed. Replicas will **diverge**. Rather than prevent that, which would mean refusing writes, we'll let it happen and make sure we can **detect and resolve** it afterwards.

items.detail: the write went to stand-ins; the read may hit the old replicas
two sides of a partition each accept an update to cart:42
so every value needs a version that says what it has seen
preventing it means refusing writes, which we said we would not do

slides.title: Versioning with vector clocks
script: Timestamps can't tell us whether two writes were **concurrent**, and server clocks drift anyway. So every value carries a **vector clock**: a small list of (node, counter) pairs, one per coordinator that has updated it.

The user adds a book through coordinator A: **v1 [A:1]**. Then a pen, also through A: **v2 [A:2]**. v2's clock is greater than or equal to v1's in every entry, so v2 **descends from** v1, and v1 can be thrown away safely.

slides.title: Concurrent versions
script: Now a partition. On one side, the user adds a mug through coordinator B: **v3 [A:2, B:1]**. On the other side, the pen is removed through coordinator C: **v4 [A:2, C:1]**. Both writes succeed.

Compare the clocks: v3 has a B entry that v4 lacks, and v4 has a C entry that v3 lacks. Neither descends from the other, so they're **concurrent siblings**, and the store **keeps both**. It never silently throws away a write it acknowledged.

slides.title: Reconciling siblings
script: On the next read, the coordinator returns **both siblings** along with their clocks. The cart service knows what a cart means, so it **merges** them, here by taking the union, and writes back **v5 [A:3, B:1, C:1]**, which descends from both and replaces them.

Notice the catch: the union brings back the **pen the user removed**. Merging adds is easy and safe; merging deletes needs more care. Amazon chose this deliberately: a deleted item reappearing is a much smaller problem than a lost **add to cart**.

slides.title: Resolving conflicts
script: There are three common ways to resolve siblings. **Last-write-wins** keeps the version with the highest timestamp; it's simple, and Cassandra uses it, but concurrent writes are **silently lost**.

**Vector clocks with application merge**, our choice for carts, never loses a write but pushes the merge into the client. **CRDTs**, data types like counters and sets with a built-in merge, give automatic merges that handle deletes correctly, at the cost of supporting only those types. We make the strategy a per-table setting.

slides.title: Read repair
script: Reads also **heal** replicas. The coordinator compares the versions it gets back; if one replica returns an older version, the coordinator writes the newest one back to it in the background.

With **R = 2** it can still answer after two replies, and then repair any laggards whose replies arrive later. Frequently read keys stay consistent through read repair alone. Rarely read keys need another mechanism.

slides.title: Background anti-entropy
script: Hints get lost and some keys are never read, so replicas still drift. The backstop is **anti-entropy**: every node periodically compares its data with the other replicas of each range it holds, and copies over whatever's missing.

The naive version would send every key and version across the network. B and C share billions of keys, almost all identical, so we need a way to find the **few that differ** while sending almost nothing.

slides.title: Merkle trees
script: That's a **Merkle tree**. Each node builds one per key range it holds. Each **leaf** is a hash of all the keys and versions in a small slice of the range, each parent is the hash of its children, and the **root** summarizes the whole range in a few bytes.
Change any one key and its leaf hash changes, which changes every hash on the path up to the root. We draw four leaves; in practice there are thousands, so each leaf covers a few thousand keys.

slides.title: Comparing two replicas
script: Node C builds the same tree over the same range. To compare, B and C exchange **just their roots**. If the roots match, which is the common case, the whole range is identical and they're done after sending a few bytes.
Here the roots differ, 9f3a against 07bd, so something inside is out of sync.

slides.title: Descending to the difference
script: So they compare the **children**. Ranges 1–2 match, so that half is skipped entirely. Ranges 3–4 differ, so they go down again and find that only **Range 4** differs.

Now they stream just the keys in Range 4 and exchange whatever versions the other side is missing. The work is proportional to **how much differs**, not how much data there is, so anti-entropy can run continuously in the background. Trees are rebuilt when vnode ownership changes, which is one more reason to keep membership changes deliberate.

slides.title: Membership by gossip
script: Everything so far assumes every node knows the ring: who's in it, their tokens, and who's up. With no master, that knowledge spreads by **gossip**. Every second, each node picks a random peer and exchanges its view of the membership, keeping whichever entry is newer.

News spreads like a rumor: after one round two nodes know, then four, then eight, so a change reaches all hundred nodes in about **seven rounds**, a few seconds. No node is special and none is a single point of failure.

slides.title: A gossip round
script: A round is cheap. B sends a **digest**: each node it knows about with a version number. D replies with the entries where its information is **newer**, and asks for the ones where B's is newer.
Here B learns that a new node G joined, and D learns that C's heartbeat has advanced. Each node also gossips its own **heartbeat counter**, which is how the cluster notices when a node goes quiet.

steps.label: every 1 s: pick a random peer
newer: G joined (tokens…); send me C

steps.note: both views now merged; ~log₂ N rounds to reach everyone

slides.title: Detecting failures
script: Each node decides **for itself** whether a peer is down. Rather than a fixed timeout, it uses a **phi accrual** detector: it learns how often a peer's heartbeats normally arrive, and its suspicion grows the longer one is overdue. Past a threshold, the peer is treated as down and the stand-ins take over.

Crucially, that's only a **local, temporary** judgement. A node is never removed from the ring because it went quiet; that would trigger huge data moves for a reboot. Permanent joins and departures are **explicit** operator actions, also spread by gossip.

marks.note: C still owns its tokens throughout

slides.title: Inside a storage node
script: Let's zoom into one node and see how it stores data. Every replica write is first **appended to a commit log** on disk and fsynced; appends are sequential, so they're fast, and the log makes the write durable before we acknowledge it.

Then the write goes into the **memtable**, a sorted structure in memory. That's the whole write path: one sequential disk write and one memory insert, with **no random disk I/O**, which suits our write-heavy workload.

slides.title: Flushing to SSTables
script: When the memtable reaches a few hundred megabytes, it's written out as an **SSTable**: a sorted, **immutable** file, again sequentially. Then the matching part of the commit log can be thrown away.
Files are never updated in place. A new version of a key just lands in a newer SSTable, and so does a delete, as a tombstone, which we'll get to.

slides.title: Compaction
script: SSTables pile up, and a key's versions end up scattered across many of them. **Compaction** runs in the background, merging several SSTables into one larger sorted file and keeping only the versions that matter.

This structure is a **log-structured merge tree**, the engine behind Cassandra, RocksDB and others. The cost is **write amplification**, since each byte is rewritten a few times as it's merged, and compaction competes for disk with live traffic, so we **throttle** it to protect the p99.9.

slides.title: The read path and bloom filters
script: A read checks the **memtable** first, then the SSTables from newest to oldest. Opening every file would be slow, so each SSTable has a **bloom filter** in memory: a compact bit array that answers "definitely not here" or "maybe here".

At about **10 bits per key**, it's wrong only about 1% of the time, so a read usually touches **one SSTable on disk**. Add a sparse index and a block cache, and most gets are served in about a millisecond.

slides.title: Deletes are writes: tombstones
script: Deleting a key can't just remove it. If replica C missed the delete, anti-entropy would see C has the value and B doesn't, and helpfully **copy it back**. So a delete writes a **tombstone**: a marker with its own version that says this key is gone.

Tombstones flow through replication, hints and repair like any write. Compaction drops them only after a **grace period**, say 10 days, longer than any replica can be out of sync without being rebuilt.

items.detail: a tombstone with its own version, replicated like any value
a replica that missed the delete would resurrect the key via repair
reads and merges treat the key as gone if the tombstone is newest
e.g. 10 days, longer than any replica may stay out of sync

slides.title: Taming the p99.9
script: Our latency target is at the **99.9th percentile**, because a page that calls the store dozens of times hits the tail often. Waiting for the **fastest W or R of N** is the biggest lever.

We add more: if a replica is slow, send a **speculative** read to another one; let the client library pick the **least-loaded** coordinator from the preference list; and throttle compaction, repair and handoff so background work never starves live requests.

items.text: **Wait for the fastest W / R of N**
items.detail: one slow replica never slows the request
a read slower than p99 goes to another replica too; first answer wins
the client library picks among the top of the preference list
compaction, anti-entropy and hint replay yield to live traffic
memtable, bloom filters, index and block cache all in RAM

slides.title: Multiple datacenters
script: Finally, one region can fail as a whole. We run the same ring in **several datacenters**, and the preference list includes replicas in each, say 3 per datacenter. Writes are coordinated and acknowledged locally, then replicated to the other datacenters **asynchronously**.
Everything we've built still applies: hints, read repair and anti-entropy work across datacenters, and vector clocks catch the case where users in two regions update the same cart at once.

slides.title: Consistency across datacenters
script: The quorum knobs extend naturally. **Local quorum** waits for 2 of the 3 replicas in this datacenter, so latency stays in the low milliseconds and a remote outage never blocks a write; other regions catch up within about a second.

When a caller really needs it, **each quorum** waits for a majority in every datacenter, at the cost of a cross-region round trip, around 100 ms, and of availability during a partition. Carts use local quorum.

slides.title: The complete key-value store
script: Let's step back. Keys sit on a **consistent-hashing ring** with virtual nodes, each stored on **N = 3** nodes, and the coordinator waits only for the fastest **W** or **R**. **Sloppy quorums**, **hinted handoff** and **vector clocks** keep writes flowing through failures; **read repair**, **Merkle trees** and **gossip** heal the cluster with no master; and each node stores data in an **LSM tree**.

The theme throughout: we chose **availability over consistency**, and made consistency a tunable knob instead of a fixed property. That's the Dynamo idea, and it lives on in Cassandra, Riak and DynamoDB.
